passage:
The wedding band was deafening, and the man in the silk kurta kept leaning closer. "Jeevan bhai, guaranteed three percent every month. Only for the family circle. Sign tonight, the slot closes at midnight."
Jeevan heard guaranteed and tonight in the same breath, and something in him slowed down.
"Give me ten minutes," he said, and stepped out past the flower arches into the quieter car park.
He searched the firm's name on the official regulator's website. Not registered. He searched the man's name with the word complaint. Two forum posts.
Then he called Deepak, a college friend who works in audit and has nothing to sell. "Guaranteed, secret and hurry?" Deepak said. "Three warnings in one sentence. Real investments can lose money too, and no honest offer closes at midnight."
Jeevan went back in, ate his biryani, and told the man politely, "No, thank you." The man's smile vanished at once, which told Jeevan the rest.

qa.q: What return did the man promise Jeevan?
qa.a: He promised a guaranteed three percent every month.

qa.q: What did Jeevan feel when he heard guaranteed and tonight together?
qa.a: Something in him grew wary and slowed down, sensing pressure rather than a real opportunity.

qa.q: Which of Jeevan's checks worked, and why?
qa.a: Checking the regulator's website showed the firm was not registered, and calling Deepak, who had nothing to sell, gave an independent view that named the warnings.

qa.q: What does the man's vanishing smile show?
qa.a: It suggests the friendliness was only a sales tool; once Jeevan said no, there was no reason to keep it up.

grounding: A man treats guaranteed returns, secrecy and a midnight deadline as warnings, checks the regulator's registration and talks to an independent friend before saying no.

passage:
Gopika burst into the Kochi flat waving her phone. "Sabina, look! Guaranteed double in six months. The coach said to keep it quiet, only a few spots."
Sabina put down her chai. "Guaranteed double? And quiet? Let's look together before either of us puts in a rupee."
They sat on the floor with the laptop. Sabina opened the official regulator's site and searched the firm's name. Nothing. She searched the coach's name. A warning notice from last year.
"But the coach showed his results," Gopika said, deflated.
"Anyone can make a screenshot," Sabina said gently. "Real investments can go down as well as up, and they aren't sold in secret."
Gopika pulled her knees up. "I almost sent my bonus tonight."
"Almost is fine. Tomorrow let's ask someone at the bank who isn't selling anything."
Gopika laughed shakily and deleted the chat.

qa.q: What did Sabina find when she searched the coach's name?
qa.a: She found a warning notice from last year.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after seeing the search results?
qa.a: Gopika felt deflated and shaken, realising she had almost sent her bonus that night.

qa.q: What made Sabina's response helpful?
qa.a: She slowed things down, checked the official regulator's site together with Gopika, explained calmly, and suggested asking someone independent at the bank.

qa.q: What would change if Sabina had mocked Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika might have felt ashamed and defended the scheme, perhaps sending the money anyway, instead of checking calmly together.

grounding: A young woman treats a promise of guaranteed doubling and secrecy as warnings, checks the regulator with Gopika and suggests an independent opinion.

"Jyoti, trust me. Twenty percent a month. Guaranteed. My cousin's already made lakhs." Lakshmi leaned across the café table.
"Guaranteed?"
"Guaranteed. But the window closes Friday. And don't tell your family yet. They'll just worry."
Jyoti felt a small tug of excitement. Then, just as clearly, three warnings in a row: guaranteed, Friday, don't tell.
"Is the company registered with the regulator?"
"Registered? Why does that matter? It's online."
"It matters to me. Send me their full name and registration number. I'll check it on the regulator's website tonight."
"Jyoti, you think too much."
"Maybe. I'll also ask my aunt's financial adviser. She doesn't sell anything, so she has no reason to push me."
Lakshmi sighed. "By Friday it'll be full."
"Then it'll be full," Jyoti said, smiling. "Real investing has risk. And it doesn't need secrets."

qa.q: What return did Lakshmi claim?
qa.a: Twenty percent a month. Guaranteed.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when Lakshmi made the pitch?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a small tug of excitement, but also alert and wary on noticing the three warnings.

qa.q: What checks did Jyoti plan before deciding?
qa.a: Checking the company's registration on the regulator's website and asking an independent financial adviser who sells nothing.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Jyoti's caution?
qa.a: Lakshmi sees it as overthinking and worries the window will close, not recognising the pressure as a warning sign.

grounding: It shows an adult treating guaranteed returns, a deadline and secrecy as warnings, checking with the regulator and an independent adviser.

passage:
I'm Bhavna, and last year my own Gargi Masi tried to sell me a scheme.
She wasn't a crook. She believed in it completely. She showed me her passbook with "monthly returns" of fifteen percent. She said, "Beta, it's guaranteed. Put your wedding savings in before Diwali, they're closing the scheme to new people."
I love my Masi. I nearly said yes on the spot. But three things bothered me: the word "guaranteed," the rush before Diwali, and how she told me not to discuss it with my parents.
That night I looked up the scheme on the official regulator's website. It wasn't registered. Not even once.
The next weekend, I went to an independent financial planner my friend recommended. She said, "No real investment can promise fixed high returns. And when someone says hurry and keep quiet, walk away."
I showed Masi what I found. She cried. Her scheme collapsed in March.

qa.q: What monthly return did Gargi Masi's passbook show?
qa.a: Monthly returns of fifteen percent.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when her Masi pitched the scheme?
qa.a: Bhavna felt loving and tempted, nearly saying yes on the spot, but also uneasy about the warning signs.

qa.q: What steps did Bhavna take before deciding?
qa.a: She checked the scheme on the official regulator's website and consulted an independent financial planner.

qa.q: How might Gargi Masi have felt when her scheme collapsed?
qa.a: Gargi Masi likely felt shocked and heartbroken, having truly believed in it, and perhaps grateful Bhavna stayed out.

grounding: An adult recalls treating a relative's guaranteed returns and urgency as warnings, checking with the regulator and an independent planner.

passage:
Financial literacy counsellor's note, community centre, Saturday. Written by Noor.
Jeevan came in today with a printout. A colleague had offered him a place in an "exclusive gold trading scheme": guaranteed twelve percent a month, entry closing Monday, and "don't share this with too many people."
What impressed me was what he had already done. He hadn't paid anything. He had searched the scheme's name on the official regulator's website: not registered. He had asked the colleague for a company registration number: no answer.
He said, "It sounded too good, and too fast, and too quiet. So I wanted someone independent to look." I confirmed his findings and explained that real investments always carry some risk and aren't sold with secrecy.
He decided not to invest, and he's going to tell the colleague why, gently, in case the colleague has put in money too. We also reported the scheme to the cyber police together.

qa.q: What return did the gold trading scheme guarantee?
qa.a: Guaranteed twelve percent a month.

qa.q: How did Jeevan seem to feel about the offer?
qa.a: Jeevan seemed cautious and uneasy, sensing it was too good, too fast and too quiet.

qa.q: What checks had Jeevan already done?
qa.a: He searched the scheme on the official regulator's website, asked for a registration number, and came to an independent counsellor before paying.

qa.q: How might the colleague feel when Jeevan explains?
qa.a: The colleague might feel surprised or defensive, and possibly worried if they have already put in money.

grounding: A counsellor notes an adult treating guaranteed returns and urgency as warnings, checking with the regulator and seeking independent advice.

passage:
Sunday night
Ishita called again about her uncle's scheme: "Guaranteed returns, better than any bank, but only for people who join this week, and don't tell too many people." She's my closest friend from college, and she's so excited that I nearly said yes just not to disappoint her.
But three phrases kept bothering me: guaranteed, this week, don't tell. Anything real I've read about carries some risk, and nothing real needs to be kept quiet.
So instead of deciding, I looked up the scheme's name on the regulator's official website. Not registered. Then I called Mamaji, who has been a chartered accountant for years and has nothing to gain either way. He said, "Good that you paused. Don't let a deadline decide for you."
I texted Ishita: "I'm not joining, and I'm a little worried for you. Can we check it together?" She hasn't replied. That stings. But my stomach feels calm for the first time this week.
Santosh

qa.q: What did Santosh find on the regulator's official website?
qa.a: The scheme was not registered.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling after texting Ishita?
qa.a: Santosh felt stung by Ishita's silence but calm inside for the first time that week.

qa.q: Which warning signs did Santosh notice, and what did Santosh do about them?
qa.a: Guaranteed, this week and don't tell; Santosh checked the regulator's website and asked Mamaji, an independent person with nothing to gain.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel reading Santosh's message?
qa.a: Ishita may feel hurt or defensive at first, since she was excited and it is her uncle's scheme, but the offer to check together leaves room to reconsider.

grounding: Shows an adult treating guaranteed returns, a rush and secrecy as warnings, checking regulator registration and consulting someone independent.
